COMMERCIAL FINANCING DISCLOSURE LAW — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
California's Commercial Financing Disclosure Law, Financial Code sections 22800 through 22807, requires many non-bank providers of commercial financing — including factoring companies, asset-based lenders, and merchant cash advance and other online lenders — to give a written disclosure to the recipient of the financing before the transaction is consummated. The law was originally enacted as SB 1235 (2018) and has since been amended, including changes effective January 1, 2024 (SB 33) and January 1, 2026 (SB 362). This information sheet describes the law's general framework as it could apply to financing between Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee; it states facts about what the statute requires and does not determine whether the law applies to any specific offer of financing involving Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee, or complete the disclosure itself.

WHAT COUNTS AS "COMMERCIAL FINANCING"
The disclosure law applies to "commercial financing," a defined term covering an accounts receivable purchase transaction (including factoring), an asset-based lending transaction, a commercial loan, a commercial open-end credit plan, or a lease financing transaction — but only when the financing is intended by the recipient for use primarily for something other than personal, family, or household purposes. If financing from Acme, Inc. to Jordan Lee fits one of these categories and is for a business purpose, it falls within this defined term, subject to the exemptions and dollar threshold described elsewhere in this law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Commercial financing” means an accounts receivable purchase transaction, including factoring, asset-based lending transaction, commercial loan, commercial open-end credit plan, or lease financing transaction intended by the recipient for use primarily for other than personal, family, or household purposes."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22800.)
  "The provider shall not be required to ascertain that the proceeds of the commercial financing are used in accordance with the statement of intended purposes."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22800.)
  Known gap: The statute lets a provider rely on the recipient's own signed, written statement of intended use to determine whether financing is "commercial" rather than personal, family, or household in nature, and does not require the provider to verify that the proceeds were actually used that way. This document doesn't determine what use the recipient intends for any particular financing, or whether a signed purpose statement exists for it — both are facts specific to the transaction.

DOLLAR THRESHOLD FOR A COVERED "RECIPIENT"
The disclosure law only reaches offers presented to a "recipient" as the statute defines that term: a person presented a specific commercial financing offer that is equal to or less than $500,000. An offer above that amount is outside the disclosure law's coverage, regardless of what kind of commercial financing is involved.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Recipient” means a person who is presented a specific commercial financing offer by a provider that is equal to or less than five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000)."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(n) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22800.)
  "“Commercial loan” means a loan of a principal amount of five thousand dollars ($5,000) or more, or any loan under an open-end credit plan, the proceeds of which are intended by the recipient for use primarily for other than personal, family, or household purposes."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22800.)
  Known gap: This $500,000 ceiling on the "recipient" definition is a separate figure from the $5,000 floor that appears in the statute's definition of a "commercial loan" specifically; that $5,000 figure only sets the minimum principal amount for a loan to count as a "commercial loan" and does not set a floor on disclosure coverage generally — financing structured as an accounts receivable purchase, lease financing, or open-end credit plan is not subject to that $5,000 minimum. This document doesn't calculate the dollar amount of any specific offer to the recipient or confirm it falls at or under the $500,000 ceiling.

TRANSACTIONS AND PROVIDERS EXEMPTED FROM THE DISCLOSURE LAW
The disclosure law does not apply to a provider that is itself a depository institution (a bank, savings association, or credit union) or a federal Farm Credit Act lender, to a commercial financing transaction secured by real property, to certain vehicle-dealer financing of at least $50,000, or to a provider that makes only one commercial financing transaction in California in a 12-month period, or that makes five or fewer such transactions in that period where they are incidental to that provider's business.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any person who makes no more than one commercial financing transaction in California in a 12-month period or any person who makes five or fewer commercial financing transactions in California in a 12-month period that are incidental to the business of the person relying upon the exemption."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22801(a),(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22801.)
  "“Provider” also includes a nondepository institution, which enters into a written agreement with a depository institution to arrange for the extension of commercial financing by the depository institution to a recipient via an online lending platform administered by the nondepository institution."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(m) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22800.)
  Known gap: The depository-institution exemption applies to the entity that is itself a bank, savings association, or credit union — it does not automatically exempt a separate, nondepository company that arranges financing on a bank's behalf. The statute's definition of "provider" expressly reaches a nondepository institution that enters a written agreement with a depository institution to arrange for the depository institution's extension of commercial financing through an online lending platform the nondepository institution administers. Whether a particular provider is itself a depository institution, arranges financing for one under such an agreement, or fits one of the other listed exemptions is a fact this document doesn't determine.

REQUIRED DISCLOSURE CONTENT AND TIMING
A provider subject to the law must disclose the total amount of funds provided, the total dollar cost of the financing, the term or estimated term, the method, frequency, and amount of payments, a description of prepayment policies, and the total cost of the financing expressed as an annualized rate. The disclosure must be given at the time the provider extends a specific commercial financing offer, and the provider must obtain the recipient's signature on the disclosure before consummating the transaction — meaning Acme, Inc., if it is a covered provider, cannot close a covered transaction with Jordan Lee until Jordan Lee has signed the disclosure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A provider subject to this division shall disclose all of the information in subdivision (b) or in Section 22803, if applicable, to a recipient at the time of extending a specific commercial financing offer to that recipient, and shall obtain the recipient’s signature on the disclosure before consummating the commercial financing transaction."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22802(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22802.)
  "(1) The total amount of funds provided. (2) The total dollar cost of the financing. (3) The term or estimated term. (4) The method, frequency, and amount of payments. (5) A description of prepayment policies. (6) The total cost of the financing expressed as an annualized rate."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22802(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22802.)
  Known gap: The statute names these six disclosure items but does not itself define how each is calculated or formatted — that detail is delegated to regulations the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation must adopt, described in a separate clause of this document. This document verifies only the Financial Code statutory text; it does not independently verify the commissioner's current implementing regulations, which supply the operative definitions, calculation methods, and formatting requirements for each disclosure item.

ALTERNATIVE DISCLOSURE FOR FACTORING AND ASSET-BASED LENDING
A provider offering factoring or asset-based lending under a general agreement — one that describes the general terms and conditions of the financing that will occur under it, rather than a single specific transaction — may give an alternative, example-based disclosure instead of the standard six-item disclosure. That alternative illustrates, for a given amount of accounts receivable, what an amount financed, total dollar cost, term, payment method and amount, prepayment policy, and annualized rate would look like for a transaction under the general agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "As an alternative to the disclosures required in subdivision (b) of Section 22802, a provider who offers commercial financing that is factoring or asset-based lending and that offers the recipient an agreement that describes the general terms and conditions of the commercial financing transaction that will occur under the agreement, may provide the following disclosures as an example of a transaction that could occur under the general agreement for a given amount of accounts receivables"
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22803 (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22803.)
  Known gap: This alternative is optional ("may provide") and is available only to a factoring or asset-based lending provider using a general agreement of this kind; it is not available to other kinds of commercial financing, and a factoring or asset-based lending provider that doesn't use a qualifying general agreement must still use the standard disclosure. This document doesn't determine which disclosure approach a particular provider used or is required to use for any specific transaction.

DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS DEPEND ON COMMISSIONER REGULATIONS
The statute directs the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation to adopt regulations defining and setting calculation and format requirements for each disclosure item, including the annualized rate disclosure. By the statute's own terms, a provider is not required to comply with the disclosure requirements at all until the commissioner's final regulations are adopted and become effective.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The commissioner shall adopt regulations governing the disclosures described in paragraphs (1) to (5), inclusive, of subdivision (b) of Section 22802 and subdivisions (a) to (e), inclusive, of Section 22803."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22804(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22804.)
  "A provider shall not be required to comply with the disclosure requirements of this division until the final regulations are adopted by the commissioner pursuant to this section and become effective on the applicable date described in Section 11343.4 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22804(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22804.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn solely from the Financial Code text fetched from the California Legislative Information website; it does not independently verify the commissioner's actual regulations (which would appear in the California Code of Regulations, not the Financial Code) or confirm their current effective status. Separately, a lightweight CourtListener case-law search performed for this document returned a 429 quota-exceeded response (125 requests/day limit) before any case law could be checked, so this entire document is statute-only — no judicial interpretation of any provision of this law was reviewed, and the gaps identified here rest only on the statutory text itself.

APR TERMINOLOGY, SAFE HARBOR, AND ENFORCEMENT
The law also addresses how providers may describe financing cost outside the required disclosure itself, and how the disclosure law is enforced. A provider is barred from using the term "interest" or "rate" in a way that could reasonably mislead a recipient, and once a provider states a charge, pricing metric, or financing amount for a specific offer during an application process, it must also state the annual percentage rate using the term "annual percentage rate" or the acronym "APR." No provision of the law imposes liability on a provider solely because the actual APR later charged differs from an estimated APR that was disclosed consistent with the commissioner's regulations, orders, or written interpretive opinions. A violation by a provider licensed under the California Financing Law is treated as a California Financing Law violation, and a violation by a provider not subject to that law is treated as an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice under the California Consumer Financial Protection Law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A provider shall not use the term “interest” or “rate” in a deceptive way that could reasonably result in the recipient being misled."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22806(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22806.)
  "No provision of this division imposes any liability on a provider as a result of the actual Annual Percentage Rate (APR) charged by a provider differing from the Estimated APR disclosed in conformity with any regulation, order, or written interpretive opinion of the commissioner or any such opinion of the Attorney General"
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22805 (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22805.)
  "A violation of this division by a person licensed under the California Financing Law (Division 9 (commencing with Section 22000)) shall be deemed a violation of the California Financing Law if the violation relates to a commercial financing transaction that is subject to the California Financing Law."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22807(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Financial Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22807.)
  Known gap: The anti-deception, APR-terminology, and enforcement provisions cited here (Financial Code sections 22806 and 22807, and the current section 22805) were added or renumbered by SB 362, effective January 1, 2026 — they go well beyond the disclosure mechanics of the original 2018 SB 1235 enactment that the research brief for this document was framed around, and are recent enough that this document did not find (and did not attempt to search for, given the CourtListener quota limit noted elsewhere in this document) any court decisions interpreting them. Section 22805 itself was renumbered from former Section 22806 by that same 2025 legislation, so a reader consulting an older source that cites "Financial Code section 22806" for the APR safe-harbor rule is looking at a since-superseded section number for that particular rule.
